extracted.intended_audience: cognitive neuroscientists, social psychologists, and neuroimaging researchers studying humor, emotion, and individual differences
extracted.subtask_short: fMRI study of point-to-self aggressive humor
extracted.subtask_description: Designing, running, analyzing, and reporting an event-related fMRI experiment that compares point-to-self aggressive vs. non-aggressive and humorous vs. non-humorous stimuli, including behavioral ratings (funniness, anger) and individual-differences moderators (self-control, self-construal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of funniness (behavioral rating)
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree of funniness was measured by participant ratings and expressed on a 0–100 linear score (higher = funnier). Scores were summed across 25 trials per condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original data used a two-point scale during scanning and a nine-point scale for re-rating; re-rating scores were adjusted to a linear 0–100. Re-rating was scheduled 1 week after fMRI to avoid repeated-reading effects and to obtain more detailed/stable evaluations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of anger (behavioral rating)
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree of anger was measured by participant ratings and expressed on a 0–100 linear score (higher = angrier). Scores were summed across 25 trials per condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Same measurement/adjustment procedure as funniness: two-point during scanning, nine-point on re-rating converted to 0–100; re-rating scheduled 1 week later to reduce repetition effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: 2 × 2 experimental stimulus classification (AH, AnH, nAH, nAnH)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stimuli are classified along two within-subjects factors — humor (humorous vs. non-humorous) and aggression (aggressive vs. non-aggressive) — yielding four conditions: AH (aggressive + humorous), AnH (aggressive + non-humorous), nAH (non-aggressive + humorous), nAnH (non-aggressive + non-humorous).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design is used to isolate effects of humor and aggression and their interaction; the paper emphasizes considering the social attribute/direction of humor (point-to-self vs point-to-other) when constructing stimuli.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical analysis: repeated-measures and mixed ANOVA
rubrics_metrics.description: Use repeated-measures ANOVA for within-subject factors (humor, aggression) and mixed ANOVA when including between-group variables (self-control, self-construal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report F, p, effect size (η²), and observed power. Test main effects and interactions (two-way and three-way) and follow up with simple main effects where interactions are significant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-rating procedure to improve measurement granularity
rubrics_metrics.description: Re-rate stimuli on a more granular scale (nine-point) at a later session to obtain more stable and detailed evaluations than brief in-scanner ratings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schedule re-rating sufficiently after the main task (here, 1 week) to avoid practice/repetition effects; convert to common metric (0–100) for comparisons; explicitly report descriptive statistics (means and SE).

rubrics_metrics.name: Individual differences as between-group moderators
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure personality variables (self-control, self-construal) and include them as between-group factors to examine how individual differences regulate behavioral and neural responses to aggressive humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When sample size is small, authors divided participants into high/low groups for each scale; they caution this can reduce reliability and recommend larger samples and treating scores as continuous in future work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whole-brain fMRI analysis and reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Perform whole-brain contrasts (e.g., humor vs non-humor, aggression vs non-aggression, interactions) and report activated regions with MNI coordinates, Z values, and voxel counts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present tables of main effects and interactions, include figures of activated regions, and contrast simple main effects across conditions (e.g., AH–AnH, nAH–nAnH).

rubrics_metrics.name: ROI analysis using spherical ROIs and beta values
rubrics_metrics.description: Define regions of interest as 6-mm spheres centered at specified MNI coordinates (examples: [39, 45, -15]; [60, -54, 21]; [15, 30, 48]) and use ROI beta values as dependent variables in ANOVAs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ROI beta values to test interactions with between-group individual differences (self-control, self-construal) and to probe hypothesized functional roles (e.g., anger control, self-cognition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrast reporting of lateralization and common vs. specific activations
rubrics_metrics.description: Report both common activations across humor types (e.g., left inferior frontal gyrus, middle temporal gyrus) and activations specific to aggressive humor (right frontal and right temporal regions), and discuss lateralization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid over-generalizing the role of a brain region from a single humor type; analyze commonness and characteristics across humor subtypes to distinguish general vs. specific neural mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of emotional valence and self-cognition frameworks
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpret activation patterns in light of theories such as the emotional valence hypothesis (left hemisphere for positive emotion, right for negative) and the role of right-hemisphere regions in self-cognition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use theoretical frameworks to explain bilateral vs. lateralized activation patterns (e.g., AH showed bilateral activation while nAH was left-lateralized), and consider how stimulus direction (point-to-self) may recruit self-cognition networks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Event-related fMRI design to minimize confounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Use an event-related fMRI design to compare normal participants across conditions and reduce confounds present in lesion-based neuropsychological methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Event-related designs can avoid variability introduced by heterogeneous lesion locations and better isolate condition-specific activations related to humor processing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stimulus direction control (point-to-self vs point-to-other)
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly control and report the direction of aggressive humor (e.g., point-to-self) because direction can influence emotional responses and neural processing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors note prior inconsistent findings may stem from neglecting direction; future studies should manipulate and report direction as a key stimulus attribute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sample size and measurement reliability considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge and report sample size limitations and the potential unreliability of psychometric scales (e.g., self-construal) when sample is small.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When constrained by MRI logistics, avoid overextending conclusions (e.g., splitting continuous measures into high/low groups affects stability). Recommend increasing sample size and using continuous measures in future studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavioral interpretation principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpret behavioral effects with reference to psychological theories: here, aggression reduced funniness, humor reduced anger, and findings relate to superiority theory and social adaptation of humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss how findings may reconcile prior inconsistent results, emphasize the role of humor as a high-level social communication skill that can alleviate interpersonal conflict, and consider the directionality of humor when generalizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency: data availability and ethical compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Declare data availability (raw data made available to qualified researchers) and report ethics approval and written informed consent per the Declaration of Helsinki.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include statements on data sharing, ethics committee approval, and conflict-of-interest declarations to meet research transparency and ethical standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neurobehavioral linking: correlate neural activation with individual differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Test whether activation in specific brain regions (e.g., right orbital inferior frontal gyrus, right superior temporal gyrus, right superior frontal gyrus) correlates with individual differences (self-control, self-construal) to support functional interpretations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use mixed ANOVAs on ROI beta values and compare activation patterns between groups (high vs low self-control; independent vs interdependent self-construal) to infer roles like anger control or self-cognition involvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow-up analyses for significant interactions
rubrics_metrics.description: When interactions (e.g., humor × aggression, or three-way with self-construal) are significant, perform simple main effect analyses and subgroup comparisons to clarify which condition differences drive the interaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors performed simple main effects (e.g., differences between AH and AnH, nAH and nAnH) and reported significance, effect sizes, and power for these follow-ups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caveat against overgeneralization from specific methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Be cautious about generalizing neural localization claims from methods with inherent limitations (e.g., small sample, grouped continuous measures, specific stimulus types).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommend replication with larger samples, continuous-variable analyses, and varied stimulus sets to substantiate claims about neural mechanisms and lateralization.
